title: Salesforce Shares Retrace 64% of JPMorgan Surge Ahead of Crucial 4.7-Point Growth Benchmark - TechStock²
content: SAN FRANCISCO, August 14, 2026, 17:40 PDT — U.S. cash markets remained shut. Shares of Salesforce, Inc. NYSE:CRM slipped 2.6% to $196.21 on Friday. This decline came after a 4.2% gain on Thursday, which was sparked by an upbeat initiation from J.P. Morgan. The reversal was significant, wiping out roughly 64% of the previous session’s $8.04 advance. Investors initially responded positively to the fresh $250 target, but soon shifted focus back to concerns over execution. J.P. Morgan’s Samik Chatterjee assigned an Overweight rating to Salesforce, stating that concerns about AI disruption are “overblown” and establishing a $250 price target for December 2027. This projection is 27.4% higher than the stock’s closing value on Friday. MarketWatch Salesforce will release its fiscal second-quarter earnings after the close on August 26. The company’s management will hold a webcast at 5 p.m. EDT. The opening quarter established a strong benchmark. Revenue increased 13% to $11.13 billion. Current remaining performance obligations expanded 14% to $33.6 billion, and the non-GAAP operating margin was 34.8%. President and chief financial officer Robin Washington stated that Salesforce maintains confidence in “organic revenue acceleration in the second half of FY27.” The August guidance should keep this trajectory intact. The arithmetic challenge persists. Salesforce projects 11% reported growth and holds a 34.3% margin, totaling 45.3%. This results in a 4.7-point shortfall compared to the Rule of 50. Informatica adds roughly three points from growth, further widening the organic gap. Wall Street keeps a positive stance, though timelines and expectations vary. Recent published moves range from Neutral to Overweight. On August 13, Monness increased its price target to $222. UBS lifted its target to $210 the previous day, maintaining a Neutral stance. The divided moves reflect earnings as evidence rather than a conclusion. The broader market provided minimal backing on Friday. The S&P 500 slipped 0.17%, pressured by lackluster retail sales and concerns over tensions in the Middle East, which dampened risk appetite. Shares of Salesforce lagged, trailing the index by roughly 2.4 percentage points. Risks: Enterprise budgets may decelerate, with AI technologies potentially affecting software price levels. Informatica’s integration may mask underlying organic expansion. Salesforce has additionally taken on $25 billion in debt to expedite its buyback, which limits cash-flow flexibility. Investors expect the August 26 report to not only surpass quarterly forecasts, but also demonstrate that growth in AI revenue and core subscriptions can bridge the 4.7-point gap while maintaining margins. Attracting and keeping talent shapes how well the firm executes, and compensation moves in step with the fortunes of the business. As automation reshapes routine work, the mix of skills the bank needs is shifting toward technology, data, and specialized advice. Managing that transition thoughtfully, retraining where possible and hiring for new capabilities, is a challenge the entire industry shares. The culture that binds such a large organization together also matters, since consistency of service across thousands of locations and countless digital touchpoints depends on shared standards. How the firm navigates this human dimension is a quiet but important part of its story. Because JPMorgan Chase touches so much of American commerce, its own activity doubles as a barometer for the wider economy. Patterns in spending, borrowing, saving, and repayment across its enormous customer base reveal how households and businesses are faring in near real time. When card spending stays brisk and loans perform, it points to steady conditions; when caution creeps in, the bank often sees it early. This vantage point gives the lender a distinctive role in market conversation, since its observations about consumer health and business confidence carry weight. title: JPMorgan Spots Something Unusual in Hot Stocks - TradingView
content: J.P. Morgan JPM says one of Wall Street's hottest trades has developed an unusual valuation advantage: momentum stocks are now cheaper than the broader S&P 500 on a forward earnings basis. The reversal matters because investors historically have paid a premium for stocks with the strongest price trends, meaning today's setup potentially combines positive momentum with valuations that no longer look stretched. According to J.P. Morgan Equity Strategy & Quantitative Research, the forward P/E spread between momentum stocks and the S&P 500 has fallen to negative 0.3 times, placing it in just the 4.1st percentile historically. The long-term median spread is 1.8 times. That represents a dramatic reversal from 2020 and 2021, when momentum stocks commanded a forward P/E premium of more than 10 times. Importantly, cheap momentum today does not simply mean high-growth technology stocks. J.P. Morgan's list includes several cyclical and value-oriented companies trading at relatively low earnings multiples. HF Sinclair carries a 6.64 times forward P/E, Global Payments trades at 6.92 times and Marathon Petroleum at 6.94 times. Valero, APA and Phillips 66 also sit below nine times forward earnings. The valuation signal comes after another strong period for the factor. J.P. Morgan Asset Management said equity momentum stood out during the second quarter, helping drive markets higher even as value and quality factors faced tougher conditions. Momentum itself has become an important force behind the 2026 market rally, with J.P. Morgan previously highlighting strong earnings and continued price leadership as key supports. For investors, the unusual part of J.P. Morgan's finding is not simply that momentum is working. It is that investors are no longer paying the historical premium to own it. That could provide some valuation protection if earnings remain resilient. But momentum strategies can reverse quickly when market leadership changes. Investors should therefore watch earnings revisions, sector rotation and whether low-multiple leaders such as refiners, financials and industrial stocks continue outperforming. A broadening rally would strengthen the setup by reducing reliance on a handful of technology winners. The key risk is a sharp factor reversal. If economic conditions, interest-rate expectations or earnings trends change enough to disrupt current winners, cheap valuations alone may not prevent momentum stocks from falling. title: JPMorgan Resets Knicks Valuation After Lakers Deal - TradingView
content: Madison Square Garden Sports MSGS is getting a powerful new valuation signal after JPMorgan estimated the New York Knicks are worth $11.75 billion, following a record-setting Los Angeles Lakers transaction that reset expectations for marquee NBA franchises. The comparison matters because MSG Sports' entire public-market value is only about $9.8 billion, even though the company owns both the Knicks and NHL's New York Rangers. MSG Sports is a publicly traded professional-sports holding company whose core assets are the Knicks and Rangers, along with development-league teams and a training facility. Its economics are driven by ticket sales, league distributions, sponsorships, suites, merchandise and local media rights. JPMorgan JPM analyst David Karnovsky said, The Lakers are the most relevant comp for the Knicks in our view, given the large DMA [media market], lack of arena ownership, and still significant RSN [regional sports network] fees. He added that the Lakers deal validated the market for marquee NBA franchises. The comparison follows an agreement by Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner to acquire control of the Lakers at a $12.5 billion valuation, about a year after Mark Walter took majority control at a $10 billion valuation. For MSGS investors, the implied discount is difficult to ignore. JPMorgan's $11.75 billion estimate for the Knicks alone exceeds MSG Sports' current market capitalization before assigning meaningful value to the Rangers or other assets. The operating business is also growing. Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue rose 37% to $278.7 million, helped by playoff-related revenue, league distributions, sponsorship and merchandise. The key question is whether private-market franchise valuations can eventually close MSGS' public-market discount. Investors should watch any strategic moves involving team ownership, share structure or asset separation, along with Knicks playoff performance and NBA media-rights economics. The league's new national media agreements are already boosting distributions to MSG Sports. The biggest limitation is that the Knicks are not currently for sale, so an $11.75 billion appraisal does not automatically translate into shareholder value. Still, another premium NBA transaction near or above the Lakers' valuation would strengthen the argument that MSGS shares materially understate the value of the assets they represent. title: Salesforce Stock Drops 2.8% as JPMorgan AI Bounce Vanishes - TradingView
content: Salesforce CRM, the enterprise-software giant behind one of corporate America's biggest customer platforms, surged more than 4% Thursday after JPMorgan JPM came out swinging for the stock. Analyst Samik Chatterjee initiated coverage with an overweight rating and a $250 target, arguing Wall Street may be pricing in too much damage from generative AI. Then came Friday. Salesforce reversed roughly 2.8% in morning trading, quickly putting the AI debate back in the spotlight. The market's message is clear: investors want proof that AI will make Salesforce stronger, not obsolete. And Salesforce finally has some serious numbers to put behind that argument. Its latest quarterly results showed Agentforce and Data 360 annual recurring revenue approaching $3.4 billion, up more than 200%. Agentforce ARR alone exploded 205% to $1.2 billion, while customers burned through 3.8 billion agentic work units. That changes the conversation. AI is no longer just a future-growth story sitting inside a presentation deck. It is becoming a real business with real dollars behind it. Now Salesforce needs to show those dollars are additive rather than simply replacing traditional software subscriptions. Here is where the setup gets interesting. GuruFocus puts Salesforce at $196.20 versus a GF Value of $331.70 as of August 14, leaving the shares 40.85% below GF Value. That is a massive valuation gap, but the market clearly wants Salesforce to earn its way back. The $3.4 billion of Agentforce and Data 360 ARR already equals roughly 7.4% of the midpoint of Salesforce's $46.05 billion full-year revenue guidance, although ARR and recognized revenue are not directly comparable. JPMorgan sees the AI threat as overdone. GuruFocus sees a stock trading far below GF Value. Salesforce now has to deliver the missing piece: faster growth. August 26 could be the next big test. title: Franklin Templeton, JP Morgan AM want tokenized fund KYC on par with stablecoins - ledgerinsights.com
content: A coalition of major asset managers has asked the US Treasury and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) to modernize know your customer (KYC) rules for tokenized funds. Franklin Templeton, Janus Henderson, JP Morgan Asset Management and WisdomTree want similar treatment to stablecoins, where the GENIUS Act permits KYC to be conducted during on and off boarding but doesn’t require it for each transaction. They have formed the Coalition for Tokenized Markets (CTM). “Registered funds should have the same opportunity to compete on a level playing field. That competition is good for investors and good for U.S. capital markets,” states a July letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and FinCEN Director Andrea Gacki. They have a point. If the equivalent rules were imposed on stablecoins, every user of a stablecoin would have to go through KYC directly with the stablecoin issuer. One way to do that is by using a bullish butterfly spread. This is a similar idea to the one we looked at Thursday on Valero Energy (VLO). Butterfly spreads involve three different option strikes, all within the same expiration date, and are created using either calls or puts. By trading a butterfly with a bullish bias, we can place the trade cheaply and have a large potential payoff. One way to do this is to set a price target that you think the stock could get to over the next few weeks. Assuming we have a price target of 380 for JPM stock within the next few weeks, let's look at how we can set up a bullish butterfly based on those parameters. First, you buy one Sept. 18 call at 370 a share for $7 apiece. Then you sell two Sept. 18 calls at 380 for $3.50 each. Finally, buy one Sept. 18 call at 390 for $1.50. This trade only costs around $150 per spread on a 100-share contract, but has a payoff potential much higher than that. The ideal scenario is for JPM to be right around 380 at expiration on Sept. 18. The maximum loss on the trade is equal to the premium paid of around $150 per contract. This would occur anywhere below 370 or above 390. The maximum potential profit on the trade is $850. Calculate this by taking the width of the butterfly, or $10, multiplied by 100. Then subtract the $150 premium paid. Taking a low-risk trade like this can be one way to gain exposure to a bounce in JPMorgan Chase without risking too much capital. AlphaStreet Newsdesk powered by AlphaStreet Intelligence The Chemours Company (NYSE:CC) surged 5.4% on Friday, closing at $15.99, despite three major Wall Street firms slashing their price targets by an average of 33.8%. The specialty chemicals maker drew heavy attention as JP Morgan, BMO Capital, and UBS all issued revised outlooks, yet investors pushed shares higher on trading volume of 285,293. The catalyst came from a trio of analyst moves that painted a decidedly cautious picture. JP Morgan maintained its Neutral rating while cutting its price target from $22 to $15. BMO Capital, keeping an Outperform stance, reduced its target from $26 to $18. UBS also held its Neutral rating but slashed its target from $29 to $18. The average new price target across the three firms now sits at $17, representing modest upside from current levels but a sharp retreat from previous expectations. The counterintuitive rally highlights a disconnect between Wall Street’s revised outlook and market reaction. With a market capitalization of $2.4 billion, Chemours saw shares climb even as analysts collectively lowered their sights by more than a third. The divergence suggests investors may have already priced in the downward revisions, or that the new targets—particularly BMO’s $18 and UBS’s $18—still imply meaningful upside potential from the $15.99 close. The specialty chemicals sector has faced headwinds from cyclical demand patterns and input cost pressures, making analyst recalibrations a recurring theme. Friday’s volume suggests steady institutional interest, though not at levels indicating panic or euphoria. The fact that BMO Capital maintained its Outperform rating despite the target cut indicates at least one firm sees value at current levels, potentially emboldening buyers who view the stock as oversold. content: Putting our long-tenured investment teams on the line to earn the trust of institutional investors. AI investment is driving U.S. data center construction at a scale that demands new approaches to financing. J.P. Morgan's Investment Banking teams break down how corporate debt, project-level debt and multi-layered equity structures are being deployed — and what risks developers and investors need to manage. The U.S. data center market is experiencing unprecedented growth, fueled by the rapid adoption of AI, cloud computing and enterprise migration. In 2026 alone, J.P. Morgan estimates capex for the five largest U.S. hyperscalers — large-scale cloud and technology companies — will reach $697 billion, up by $173 billion since the beginning of the year. As John Servidea, global co-head of Investment Grade Finance at J.P. Morgan, said, “AI financing is the biggest secular theme in our professional lifetimes.” The industry ambition is visible in recent transactions. Project Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative announced by the U.S. government in January 2025, plans to invest up to $500 billion in U.S. data centers and energy infrastructure over four years. J.P. Morgan originated $9.6 billion across two construction loans for the initiative’s Abilene, Texas campus, acting as lead left, sole underwriter and sole structuring agent on both transactions — a single engagement that illustrates the scale of capital now moving into AI infrastructure. “AI financing is the biggest secular theme in our professional lifetimes.” Global co-head of Investment Grade Finance, J.P. Morgan Behind every AI model training run and cloud query sits a physical support structure: purpose-built facilities that require land, power, cooling and connectivity at industrial scale. “That’s digital infrastructure. Most people don’t realize it, but there’s billions of dollars of physical assets supporting virtually every technology experience that you enjoy today,” said Scott Wilcoxen, head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking at J.P. Morgan. Historically, this infrastructure spanned foundational physical networks including cell towers, fiber-optic cables and satellites. As AI adoption and cloud computing grow, data centers are emerging as the most critical facilities to support increased demand. Not all open land can support industrial-grade utilities and long-term expansion possibilities. Developers must closely evaluate data center build sites based on unique requirements, including: Acreage: According to IBM, the average onsite data center typically has between 2,000 and 5,000 servers, with a footprint reaching 100,000 square feet — roughly the equivalent of 38 standard tennis courts. Connection: The space must offer proximity to power transmission and fiber networks, or the project must consider installation of these connections as part of the build cost. Environmental security: Consideration of earthquakes, floods and other environmental risks is critical to ensure consistent compute capabilities with minimal interruptions. Community considerations: Developers must address concerns from communities near data center build sites prior to breaking ground. This goes beyond paperwork to include public hearings and stakeholder negotiation. Doing so is a crucial step in establishing permitting rights across zoning, building permits, water rights and more. “Data doesn’t move in a vacuum, it moves over a medium.” Head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan AI infrastructure financing requires both scale and bespoke structuring. The capital needs are large, build timelines are long, and the cash flow profile often differs from what traditional investment-grade markets are accustomed to underwriting. “What’s particularly exciting for us is the level of creativity that is required to finance all of this. Thinking about how to raise this capital in the most efficient way requires a lot of collaboration across teams and markets,” said Servidea. In AI infrastructure, debt most often comes in two core structures: corporate (balance-sheet) debt and project-level debt. Corporate debt allows for speed and flexibility: proceeds can fund capex across data center buildouts, power-related spending, networking and compute without tying the lender to one specific project’s performance. Project-level debt, by contrast, is underwritten primarily to a defined set of project cash flows, often supported by long-term contracts or otherwise high-visibility revenues. The trade-off is less flexibility and more structural complexity, in exchange for tighter lender protections and debt sizing that is anchored to the asset’s own cash generation. The June 2026 financing of Hut 8’s Beacon Point data center in Nueces County, Texas illustrates how project-level debt can be structured around durable, contracted cash flows. J.P. Morgan acted as lead left bookrunner on the $4.25 billion senior secured notes offering, which was 100% pre-leased under a 15-year triple-net lease to a high investment-grade tenant. The transaction achieved a 95% loan-to-cost ratio — the highest ever for a high-performance computing data center bond — and priced at T+165, the tightest spread ever recorded for a data center construction bond. Equity is the risk-absorbing capital in AI infrastructure, used to fund growth and shoulder uncertainties that debt investors typically discount, such as technology obsolescence, ramp-up timing, utilization volatility and customer concentration. In practice, equity is often used to get projects built and scaled, with the expectation that the business can later add more debt once revenues are contracted and performance is more predictable. As capital needs grow, equity financing structures have become increasingly complex, often drawing on multiple layers of the capital stack simultaneously. “More often, forming this capital means going to multiple pockets, across multiple regions and, in many instances, looking across multiple layers of the capital stack and incorporating both structured as well as common equity to ultimately fund these investments,” said Wilcoxen. CoreWeave’s April 2026 capital raise demonstrates how AI-first companies are increasingly drawing on multiple layers of the capital stack simultaneously. J.P. Morgan acted as lead left and active bookrunner on a $5.25 billion combined offering comprising of $1.75 billion in senior unsecured notes and $3.5 billion in convertible senior notes. This deal represents one of the largest combined high-yield and convertible offerings ever executed. It also reflects both the scale of capital required to build and operate AI infrastructure at speed and the sophistication of the financing structures now available across the sector. “Investors are not blindly buying everything. There’s a tremendous amount of capital being deployed, but investors are taking the time to do the credit work, understand the stories and figure out relative value and pricing. To me, that’s a healthy sign for the market.” Global co-head of Investment Grade Finance, J.P. Morgan As the demand for data center capacity grows, pressure builds on key components of the supply chain. According to Wilcoxen, the most crucial of these is power supply. Demand for compute is rising faster than many regional grids can support, and the friction shows up in aging transmission infrastructure, limited local capacity and multiyear wait times to connect to power that can push project timelines out materially. As a result, time to power has become a limiting factor for data center and compute deployments. “Accelerating time to power is a top priority for many of our clients, but the grid infrastructure isn’t there,” said Wilcoxen. “There’s a lot of work to do.” Beyond the grid itself, the supply chain is constrained by natural resources and physical inputs that are harder to scale quickly than capital. Builders must secure available land in the right locations, water access and cooling requirements, and appropriate permitting that determines whether a project can move from plan to energized facility. Clients are responding by securing sites and utility pathways sooner, evaluating alternative cooling approaches where feasible and bringing energy and infrastructure specialists into the diligence process to underwrite power availability and execution risk with the same rigor as the underlying compute demand. Over-building is a parallel risk: AI capital expenditure has, in many cases, outpaced monetization. “The uncertainty around how, when and in what magnitude end-user demand materializes in a monetizable way does make it difficult to plan out over a multiple-year cycle,” said Wilcoxen. As a result, long lead times for power and construction are colliding with rapidly evolving technology cycles and shifting customer needs. In response, many operators and sponsors are trying to structure buildouts in phases, pursue more contracted or pre-committed demand where possible, and maintain optionality so capacity can scale with real adoption. Debt concentration is an emerging systemic consideration as AI’s share of the overall financing market grows rapidly. “I don’t think we’re at a point yet where concentration limits are a huge concern, but it is part of the dialogue because as a portion of the overall market, AI is growing very quickly,” said Servidea. Practically, clients are working to keep funding channels resilient by diversifying capital sources, matching debt structures to cash-flow visibility and avoiding overly correlated exposures to a single counterparty, technology node or demand narrative. The throughline is that the next phase of AI infrastructure buildout will be shaped as much by execution discipline as by the availability of capital. “We’re building the physical underpinnings of the future technological progress of mankind.” Head of Global Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan Investor appetite for AI infrastructure is strong, but it’s not indiscriminate. “Investors are not blindly buying everything. There’s a tremendous amount of capital being deployed, but investors are taking the time to do the credit work, understand the stories and figure out relative value and pricing. To me, that’s a healthy sign for the market,” said Servidea. Rather than jumping on the bandwagon, investors are positioning themselves to finance a long-term buildout, considering downside protection as much as upside. “The red lights would start flashing if it felt like there was blind euphoria. That’s not what we’re seeing,” Servidea said. While AI is a major incremental driver, infrastructure buildout is broader than a single theme. “This entire AI dynamic is additive to an already extraordinarily large investment base,” said Wilcoxen. For instance, public cloud and software-as-a-service (SaaS) models are expected to expand meaningfully in the near future. Compute growth won’t map one-to-one with revenue or usage because efficiencies improve over time, but the direction of travel remains clear: more workloads, more data movement and more always-on digital services will translate into continued expansion of data centers, networks and supporting hardware. The next phase of AI infrastructure will reward platforms that can secure reliable, scalable power, navigate grid access and interconnection timelines, and structure financing around durable demand signals. If AI meaningfully reshapes products and workflows, the practical implication is sustained investment not just in compute, but in the physical and energy foundations that make that compute usable at scale. “When you think about all the different things society will be able to do with AI over the next five years, 10 years, 20 years, it’s really hard to comprehend what that’s going to ultimately require,” said Wilcoxen. “We’re building the physical underpinnings of the future technological progress of mankind.” The data center surge: Building the backbone of the digital age Our experts dive deep into the world of digital infrastructure — exploring the critical role of data centers, fiber, and towers in powering today’s digital economy. They also discuss the risks of overbuilding, and the importance of operational expertise. AI is transforming global economies and revolutionizing industries. title: JP Morgan banker who led Infantino’s Fifa sell-off has Epstein ties exposed - AOL.com
content: The JP Morgan Chase banker who was one of the secret figures behind the Fifa sell-off plan is also under pressure for her links to the late paedophile and financier Jeffrey Epstein. Mary Erdoes, 58, the head of the asset and wealth management division, led the bank’s efforts to find investors prepared to take part of the 20 per cent stake in Fifa which its president Gianni Infantino sought to sell. Erdoes has also come under scrutiny for her previous longstanding connection to Epstein, who died in 2019. Documents released by the US authorities indicate that Erdoes only ended JP Morgan’s relationship with Epstein in 2013, five years after he was convicted in Florida of procuring a minor for prostitution. Emails exchanged between the pair, first reported by The Banker financial news site, suggest that they were in contact regarding banking. Erdoes emailed Epstein birthday greetings from her JP Morgan account in 2012. The pair were in indirect contact via staff about the banking arrangements for another associate of Epstein, Kathryn Ruemmler, the former Goldman Sachs executive. Erdoes is, according to the New York Times, understood to be one of the few individuals who knew about Infantino’s plans as they were formulated. Those involved selling a 20 per cent stake in Fifa at a value of $4.2bn (£3.1bn) to investors led by Joshua Kushner – the brother of US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner – and others. Infantino did not reveal the plan to his closest staff until days before the World Cup final. Joshua Kushner’s investment vehicle, Thrive Eternal, and Fifa planned to use JP Morgan to find fellow investors for the putative sale, which was subsequently abandoned by Infantino. The Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) project caused uproar in world football and has left Infantino fighting for his future as Fifa president. The European governing body, Uefa, as well as counterparts in Asia and North and Central America have threatened to break away. Erdoes, the bank’s second-highest earner last year on $32m (£24m), has not commented on her links to Infantino. The connection between the pair is not clear, although Infantino has been on stage with Erdoes when he spoke at a staff meeting at the bank. Previously JP Morgan apologised for its role in financing the 2021 European Super League. It is yet to make any comment on its role in FFE, or the relationship between Erdoes, the bank and Infantino. In terms of Erdoes’s dealings with Epstein, JP Morgan told The Banker: “We regret any association we had with the man [Epstein], but did not help him commit his heinous crimes. “The firm filed multiple Suspicious Activity Reports beginning in 2002 but heard nothing back from the government. “Mary Erdoes made the decision to close his accounts in 2013, six years before his arrest. Mary has always held herself and her colleagues to the highest standards of integrity and trust, is consistently recognised as one of the top executives in financial services and continues to be a critically important leader of our firm.” Meanwhile, Fifa will face a further embarrassing episode on Wednesday when Omar Artan – the Somali referee refused entry to the United States for the World Cup – will take charge of Uefa’s curtain-raising Super Cup. Artan has spoken about the “very tough period” he faced when denied entry to the US at Miami International Airport in June, before what should have been the highlight of his career. Tensions were already high between Fifa and Uefa before the start of the World Cup, in which Infantino attracted further scrutiny for his role in the decision to suspend the two-match ban given to United States striker Folarin Balogun. In what was a thinly veiled move to humiliate the global governing body, Artan was named the match referee for Wednesday’s Super Cup in Salzburg between Aston Villa and Paris St-Germain. Artan said on Monday: “It was a very tough period. A lot of people have sympathy for me, because when someone has been working a lot of years and is supposed to do something, and then can’t do it, it’s very challenging. “I really appreciate the support I received throughout the world, though; I’m so grateful.” Artan, 34, was subjected to an 11-hour immigration interview before he was denied entry to the US. Somalia is one of the 12 countries on the United States travel-ban list. Infantino later admitted publicly that he was powerless to overrule the ruling from Donald Trump’s administration. The Fifa president told critics at a press conference before the World Cup to “chill and relax” about the controversy, and added: “We work on everything, we try to resolve everything, [but] immediately screaming and shouting, that’s the opposite of finding a solution.” Aleksander Ceferin, the Uefa president, reacted by appointing Artan for the Super Cup, where he will become the first African official to take charge of the European season opener. Artan added: “When we got this call it was, for me and my family, really a very, very happy moment. There’s a big Somali community in Europe and in Austria, and they are over the moon with me officiating a match like this.” Try full access to The Telegraph free today. content: Microsoft MSFT is winning a more bullish call from JPMorgan (NYSE:JPM) as accelerating Azure growth and expanding Copilot adoption strengthen the case that its massive AI infrastructure buildout is beginning to translate into higher-value software revenue. Analyst Samik Chatterjee raised his December 2027 price target to $625 from $550 while keeping an Overweight rating, pointing to potential acceleration across both Azure and Microsoft 365 Commercial Cloud. Chatterjee sees Microsoft benefiting twice from AI spending. Azure sells computing capacity to enterprises and AI companies, while Microsoft's own products, including Copilot, act as internal customers for that same infrastructure. That creates an opportunity to monetize expensive AI capacity through higher-margin software. The upside could be substantial. Chatterjee said Copilot could ultimately add between $24 billion and $41 billion of revenue, roughly seven times his current estimate, even before considering additional monetization from AI-credit sales beyond traditional per-seat licenses. Fiscal fourth-quarter Azure and other cloud-services revenue jumped 43% year over year, while Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $59.3 billion, up 27%. Microsoft also reported more than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, with net seat additions more than doubling sequentially. The spending required to support that growth remains enormous. Microsoft spent $41 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter, with roughly two-thirds directed toward shorter-lived assets such as CPUs and GPUs. Microsoft now needs to prove that AI revenue can accelerate quickly enough to justify that infrastructure bill. The next major metric is Azure growth. Management expects roughly 45% constant-currency growth in the September quarter, accelerating from Q4, while demand continues to exceed available capacity. Investors should also watch Copilot paid seats, Microsoft 365 revenue growth and cloud margins. Microsoft Cloud gross margin was 65% last quarter as AI investment pressured profitability. If Copilot adoption approaches JPMorgan's revenue opportunity while Azure maintains 40%-plus growth, the $625 target becomes easier to defend. Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. A month has gone by since the last earnings report for JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM). Shares have added about 5.3% in that time frame, outperforming the S&P 500. But investors have to be wondering, will the recent positive trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is JPMorgan Chase & Co. due for a pullback? Well, first let's take a quick look at the latest earnings report in order to get a better handle on the recent catalysts for JPMorgan Chase & Co. before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late. JPMorgan's second-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of $6.14 per share beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $5.59 by 9.8%. The bottom line was up 17.2% from $5.24 reported a year ago.Reported net revenues of $57.35 billion rose 27.7% year over year and topped the consensus mark of $49.14 billion. Strong Markets and IB activity powered core growth, while NII got support from decent loan demand.The quarter included a $4.55 billion pretax gain related to Visa shares, which added $1.27 to earnings per share. JPM also recorded $1.03 billion of gains on certain equity investments, adding 29 cents per share. Including these significant items, net income jumped 41% year over year to $21.16 billion. Markets revenues advanced 35% to $12.08 billion on elevated client activity, strong trading performance and continued financing demand in Equities. Fixed Income Markets revenues rose 6% to $6.05 billion, while Equity Markets revenue surged 86% to $6.03 billion.IB revenues increased 45% to $3.90 billion. IB fees rose 30% to $3.28 billion on higher fees across products, led by equity underwriting. Payments revenues grew 12% to $5.30 billion, while Securities Services revenues gained 17% to $1.66 billion. Reported NII increased 9.9% to $25.51 billion. NII excluding Markets was $23.68 billion, up 4%, supported by higher deposit balances, greater revolving Card Services balances and wholesale loan growth. Lower rates partly offset those benefits.Average loans expanded 10% to $1.52 trillion, while average deposits grew 7% to $2.69 trillion. The net yield on interest-earning assets was 2.40%, down from 2.43% a year earlier, showing rate pressure despite balance sheet growth. Non-interest expenses rose 15% year over year to $27.32 billion. Higher compensation, brokerage and distribution fees, marketing, technology and occupancy costs drove the increase. Still, the reported overhead ratio improved to 48% from 53% in the prior-year quarter. The provision for credit losses was $2.52 billion, down 12%. Net charge-offs (NCOs) were $2.4 billion, down $44 million, and the company recorded a $149 million net reserve build, primarily in Wholesale. Consumer & Community Banking accounted for $2.16 billion of the provision. Commercial & Investment Bank revenues climbed 27% from the prior-year quarter to $24.85 billion, while net income soared 46% to $9.68 billion. Consumer & Community Banking revenues grew 8% to $20.27 billion, led by higher Card Services NII, auto operating lease income and wealth-management fees. Segment net income rose 3% to $5.31 billion. Debit and credit card sales volume rose 10% to $535.8 billion, while active mobile customers increased 6% to 63.7 million. Asset & Wealth Management revenues climbed 19% to $6.85 billion. Assets under management reached $5.1 trillion, up 18%, aided by $50 billion of long-term net inflows.Corporate net income was $4.21 billion compared with $1.7 billion a year ago, influenced by net gain related to Visa shares and gains on certain equity investments. JPMorgan's capital position remained strong, even as ratios eased versus year-ago levels. The standardized common equity Tier 1 capital ratio was 14.1% as of June 30, 2026, compared with 15.1% a year earlier. Tangible book value per share rose 10% to $113.35. Shareholder returns stayed elevated. The bank paid a common dividend of $4 billion, or $1.50 per share, and reported $6.2 billion of common stock net repurchases during the quarter. Management expects 2026 NII of roughly $105.5 billion and NII excluding Markets of about $96.5 billion. Both metrics show increases from the prior targets.Adjusted expenses are projected at around $107.5 billion, with the increase from the prior outlook of $106 billion reflecting higher volume- and revenue-related costs. The Card Services NCO rate is now expected to be approximately 3.2%, down from the previous target of 3.4%. JPMorgan Chase & Co.'s JPM Asia-Pacific corporate banking business continues to grow strongly, with revenues rising more than 20% so far this year, JPMorgan's regional heads, Oliver Brinkmann and Kerwin Clayton, said in an interview with Reuters. Growing investments and rising intra-Asia trade are creating new opportunities, prompting JPMorgan to sustain its hiring momentum across Asia-Pacific through 2027. JPMorgan expanded its Asia-Pacific corporate banking workforce by 20% in 2025 and is close to completing another 15% increase this year, Brinkmann and Clayton said. Clayton also mentioned that the bank plans to maintain a similar hiring pace next year to support continued growth across the region. The hiring will be done to focus on mid-sized and large companies, innovation-economy businesses and financial institutions, including both bank and non-bank financial institutions. This will support JPM's growth across these segments. The continued investment in personnel will expand the company's corporate banking presence and strengthen client relationships across Asia-Pacific. JPMorgan is seeing increased corporate banking activity across the region, driven by growing investments in AI, data centers and supply-chain infrastructure. The bank is witnessing stronger activity in Taiwan, South Korea, China, Australia, Malaysia and Singapore as companies expand their investments and operations. These trends are creating additional financing needs while supporting corporate activity and cross-border investment across the region. This is providing further growth opportunities for JPMorgan's corporate banking business. Alongside these growth areas, JPMorgan is expanding its focus on trade finance and working-capital finance as intra-Asia commerce grows. Rising regional trade and supply-chain activity is driving demand for financing and other banking services, supporting growth in its corporate banking business. The increased focus is also helping JPMorgan deepen relationships with corporate clients involved in cross-border commerce and capitalize on rising trade activity across Asia. JPMorgan's strong Asia-Pacific corporate banking growth highlights the region's increasing importance to its overall business. Continued investments in AI, data centers and supply chains, coupled with rising intra-Asia trade, will support sustained demand for corporate banking services. JPMorgan's continued hiring and focus on trade and working-capital finance should further strengthen its position and support growth across the region through 2027.
